findings.title: Storage.Create failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45) instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Storage (unified store) failure as a Legacy failure in the dual-writer metrics, corrupting the error-rate dashboards/alerts that distinguish unified-storage health from legacy-storage health. The same mistake is repeated in Update (line 129).

findings.title: Storage.Update failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This duplicates the same mislabeling bug found in Create (line 45): a Storage failure is reported as a Legacy failure, which will skew metrics used to monitor the health of each backend independently.

findings.title: Wrong label value (object name instead of resource kind) passed to storage duration metric
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the successful-path metric call is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106), passing the individual object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind` (the resource kind, e.g. "playlists"). Since `name` varies per deleted object, this will create a distinct Prometheus label value per object name, causing unbounded metric cardinality and breaking any dashboards that group by resource kind for delete operations. The failure path on line 103 correctly uses `options.Kind`, confirming this is an inconsistency/bug rather than intentional.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`, the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` (line 166) instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, which is what Create, Delete, and Update use for their analogous legacy-write goroutines. This mislabels legacy-store latency/error metrics as unified-storage metrics for the delete-collection operation.

findings.title: Delete attaches the wrong logger to the context
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, a richer logger is built with `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but the context is populated with the plain `d.Log` instead: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (line 97). Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly injects the enriched `log` variable into the context. As a result, any downstream code that pulls the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` during a Delete call loses the name/kind/method structured fields, reducing traceability specifically for delete operations.

findings.title: Async legacy writes derive their timeout context from the request context, which is canceled once the handler returns
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 51, 110, 135, 163) each spawn a goroutine that does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` using the inbound request `ctx` as the parent. For an HTTP server, the request context is canceled once the handler (ServeHTTP) returns; since these methods return the Storage result to the caller immediately after launching the goroutine (without waiting), the apiserver handler will typically finish and the request context will be canceled shortly afterward — well before the 10 second timeout and often before the legacy write even completes. Because cancellation propagates to the derived timeout context, the "safety measure" asynchronous write to legacy storage can be silently aborted on effectively every request, defeating the purpose of mode 3's async legacy write. The goroutine should detach from request cancellation (e.g. use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) before applying its own timeout.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are silently swallowed (no logging) in async goroutines
findings.body: In the async legacy-write goroutines for Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166), the only outcome recorded on failure is a boolean passed into the duration metric (`d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`); none of them call `log.Error(...)` the way the previous Mode3 implementation did (e.g. "could not update object in legacy store"). Operators now have no way to see which object/resource failed to replicate to legacy storage except by correlating metrics, substantially reducing observability for a feature explicitly intended as a safety net against unified-storage/legacy divergence.

findings.title: Update no longer guarantees the same resolved object is written to both stores
findings.body: The previous Mode3.Update implementation fetched the current object from Storage, resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and wrapped the already-resolved object so that both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update applied the exact same final object. The new implementation instead calls `d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` and then, in the async goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same unresolved `objInfo` (line 139). Each backend will internally invoke `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own "old" object; for patch-style updates (merge patch, strategic merge patch, JSON patch) this can produce two different resulting objects if the legacy store's and unified store's current state differ even slightly, causing silent divergence between the two stores — the exact problem dual-writing is meant to prevent. Additionally, invoking `UpdatedObject` a second time may not be safe/idempotent for all `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations.

findings.title: TestMode3_Delete never mocks Legacy.Delete even though it is always invoked
findings.body: DualWriterMode3.Delete unconditionally spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Delete(...)` after a successful Storage.Delete. The `testCase` struct in TestMode3_Delete only has a `setupStorageFn` field (no `setupLegacyFn`), so for the "deleting an object in the unified store" success case the legacy mock (`m := &mock.Mock{}`, never associated with `t` via `.Test(t)`) has no registered expectation for `Delete`. Calling an unmocked method on a `testify` mock without `.Test(t)` set panics; since this call happens in a background goroutine, an unrecovered panic there crashes the entire test binary non-deterministically, rather than failing just this test. The test needs to register a Legacy.Delete expectation (and ideally await/verify the call) for success cases.

findings.title: TestMode3_DeleteCollection never mocks Legacy.DeleteCollection even though it is always invoked
findings.body: Same issue as in TestMode3_Delete: DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection always spawns a goroutine calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` after a successful Storage.DeleteCollection, but the `testCase` struct here only defines `setupStorageFn`; there is no `setupLegacyFn` and no `m.On("DeleteCollection", ...)` registered on the legacy mock for the success case. The unmocked call made from the background goroutine will panic in testify's mock (since the mock is not bound to `t`), risking an unrecovered panic that crashes the test process.

findings.title: No test waits for or verifies the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs
findings.body: None of the Mode3 tests (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the async legacy write, nor do they call `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` to confirm `Legacy.*` was actually invoked. Since the goroutine may run after the subtest has already returned, the tests effectively never verify the core new behavior this PR introduces (asynchronous write-through to legacy storage as a safety measure); a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would not be caught by this test suite.

Having a duplicate checksum line suggests the file was not cleanly regenerated via `go work sync`/tooling, which can mask inconsistencies in a manually-edited lock file.
